## The premise

::: {.callout-quote}
"Riding a bicycle should not require bravery."
:::

- The principal reason why people don't ride is **fear of motor vehicle traffic** — not other cyclists, pedestrians, or solo falls
- High-cycling cities (NL, DK, DE) **removed the fear** of cycling
- In the Netherlands, a quarter of trips by people 75+ are by bike (riding "alongside seven-year-olds")

::: {.notes}
Ask: who in this room has been told they're "brave" for biking in Chicago? That comment is the phenomenon Geller is describing.
:::

## The four types

![](images/four_types_bar.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.type-card .sf-card}
**Strong & Fearless** · <1%<br>Ride regardless of conditions; cycling is identity
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.type-card .ec-card}
**Enthused & Confident** · 7%<br>Will share the road, but prefer bike lanes & boulevards
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.type-card .ic-card}
**Interested but Concerned** · 60%<br>Like riding; afraid of cars. Would ride if streets felt safe
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.type-card .nw-card}
**No Way No How** · 33%<br>Not interested in cycling *for transportation* (topography, inability, disinterest)
:::
:::
::::

# Part 1 · Take the survey {background-color="#1b1b1a"}

Answer honestly for **you, today, in Chicago** (or wherever you may be located). 

## Section A · About you

::: {.qbox}
[A1]{.qid} Are you physically able to ride a bicycle (any kind, including adaptive or e-bike)?  **Yes / No**
:::

::: {.qbox}
[A2]{.qid} *"I would like to travel by bicycle more than I do now."*<br>
1 Strongly disagree · 2 Disagree · 3 Agree · 4 Strongly agree
:::

::: {.qbox}
[A3]{.qid} In the past 30 days, did you ride a bicycle (own bike, Divvy, e-bike) **to get somewhere** — class, work, errands — not only for exercise or fun?  **Yes / No**
:::

::: {.qbox}
[B1]{.qid} What **most** keeps you from biking more? *(pick one)*<br>
Traffic / drivers · Distance · Weather · No bike · Bike theft / parking · Arriving sweaty · Don't know good routes · Personal security · Other
:::

::: {.notes}
B1 is not used in scoring. It lets us test Geller's central claim — that fear of traffic is the dominant barrier — against our own data.
:::

## Section S · How comfortable would you feel?

For each street on the next five slides, rate how comfortable you would feel **riding a bicycle there**:

::: {.scale}
[**1** Very uncomfortable]{} [**2** Somewhat uncomfortable]{} [**3** Somewhat comfortable]{} [**4** Very comfortable]{}
:::

<br>

- Imagine a typical weekday afternoon, good weather, a trip you actually need to make
- Rate the **street**, not your destination
- Go with your first reaction

## S1 · Major street, no bike lane

![](images/s1_major_no_lane.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.scale}
[**1** Very uncomfortable]{} [**2** Somewhat uncomfortable]{} [**3** Somewhat comfortable]{} [**4** Very comfortable]{}
:::

[Think: a four-lane arterial like Western or Ashland Ave, 30–35 mph, parked cars on your right.]{.tiny}

## S2 · Major street with a painted bike lane

![](images/s2_major_painted_lane.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.scale}
[**1** Very uncomfortable]{} [**2** Somewhat uncomfortable]{} [**3** Somewhat comfortable]{} [**4** Very comfortable]{}
:::

[Same street and traffic; a striped lane between moving traffic and parked cars (watch for opening doors).]{.tiny}

## S3 · Major street with a protected bike lane

![](images/s3_major_protected_lane.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.scale}
[**1** Very uncomfortable]{} [**2** Somewhat uncomfortable]{} [**3** Somewhat comfortable]{} [**4** Very comfortable]{}
:::

[Same street; the bike lane runs curbside, separated by posts and a row of parked cars (e.g., Dearborn St downtown).]{.tiny}

## S4 · Quiet residential street / neighborhood greenway

![](images/s4_residential_greenway.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.scale}
[**1** Very uncomfortable]{} [**2** Somewhat uncomfortable]{} [**3** Somewhat comfortable]{} [**4** Very comfortable]{}
:::

[One lane each way, 20 mph, few cars, speed humps and bike markings.]{.tiny}

## S5 · Off-street path or trail

![](images/s5_offstreet_path.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.scale}
[**1** Very uncomfortable]{} [**2** Somewhat uncomfortable]{} [**3** Somewhat comfortable]{} [**4** Very comfortable]{}
:::

[No cars at all — shared with people walking and running (e.g., the Lakefront Trail).]{.tiny}

# Part 2 - Score it

![](images/scoring_tree.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

[Rule-based classification adapted from Dill & McNeil (2013). Apply the steps **in order**; stop at the first type you reach.]{.tiny}

::: {.notes}
Order matters. Someone very comfortable on S1 is S&F even if they also love paths. IBC is still partly a residual category, exactly as in Geller — but now it has a positive definition: interested, able, and NOT very comfortable even with a painted lane.
:::
